reason: The court used the fiscal conveyance finding as part of its holding, but the statement drops the material limits that this was the particular conveyance and that there was no proof of temple funds or dedication.
The judgment held that section 20 applies only to sangika property formally dedicated to the priesthood, and the quote directly supports that holding.
The court said this plaint gave full details; it did not lay down a rule that a plaintiff must give full details of respondents' conduct in every lawsuit.
The quoted passage records the pleaded cause of action in this plaint, not an independent legal rule that such a cause of action may generally arise.
The court did decide there was one cause of action, but only because the deed-invalidation relief was consequential to the declaration of title and possession claim.
The judgment directly held that section 760A does not prescribe the mode of application and accepted an affidavit-only substitution application.
The court held that the original plaint should have been rejected under sections 46(2)(a) and 41 because the encroached portion was not sufficiently described.
The statement is an overbroad abstraction from the citation to sections 46 and 41 rather than a rule actually decided by the court.
The court required section 93 notice where an amended plaint was filed after a plan was prepared during an ex parte trial, a material condition missing from the statement.
The consent of residents was part of the factual background, not a holding that written resident consent is legally required for roadway changes.
The court treated R2 and X1C as non-notarial documents affecting land, but the statement omits that their validity was contestable under the Prevention of Frauds and Urban Councils Ordinance context.
The judgment held the opposite practical point: the dispute concerned all signatories and adjoining owners, so their presence was necessary.
The difference between the surveyor's report and oral evidence was a case-specific evidentiary finding, not the ratio as a legal rule.
The court relied on a material omission in this surveyor's report; it did not state a general duty that every surveyor's report must include all relevant facts.
The standard of proof holding was limited to contempt proceedings, while the statement incorrectly generalizes it to any case.
The court recognized the prior transfer of the fiduciary life interest, but the statement omits the Abolition of Fideicommissa and Entails Act and life-interest context.
The court dealt with Bibsie's specific transfer of a life interest, not a general proposition that execution of any deed transfers the original entitlement to third parties.
The judgment vested title in ultimate transferees of the life interest, whereas the statement says transferors and is materially inaccurate.
The quote supports a factual finding that the company had not commenced business, but the statement recasts it as a vague evidentiary rule.
The court treated continuation rather than winding up as a mixed question of fact and law, but the statement omits the winding-up discretion and burden context.
The court only said there was no point first agitating in the domestic forum because the 73 percent majority opposed winding up, not that a winding-up order should not be sought.
The judgment directly held that an executor is not functus officio until the administration of the estate is duly completed.
The court held that even a reprehensible 33-month delay did not justify reversal without demonstrated prejudice or failure of justice.
The judgment treated the will reference as an acknowledgment of Lot 11's existence, not as a legal admission of the testator's rights to the property.
The court applied the rule that contractual intention governs the object of the obligations when deciding whether specific performance was available.
